title: Bhai Daya Singh
hookLine: the first to rise at Anandpur, who later, tradition says, carried the Zafarnama

lines: A SWORD, AND A HARD QUESTION.
cards: Every room has that silence. A teacher asks for a volunteer, a manager asks who'll take the hard job, and nobody moves. Everyone looks at their shoes and waits for someone else.
Now make it a hillside at Anandpur, a great crowd, and a Guru with a drawn sword asking for a head. The silence must have been enormous. Then one man stands up.
He doesn't know what's in the tent. He doesn't know that four more will follow him. He just rises, first, alone.

teach.b: Before that day he was Daya Ram, and tradition says he came from Lahore. When Guru Gobind Singh called for someone ready to give his head, he answered first.
He walked into the tent. Four others followed, one at a time. And all five walked out again, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved, the first members of the Khalsa.
Daya Ram became Daya Singh. Being first is a strange gift. The second person to stand up still has to be brave.
But the first stands into total uncertainty, with no one ahead of him to show it can be survived. Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh for that rising, and his story didn't end there.
He stayed close to the Guru through the hard years that followed.

Then, tradition says, the Guru wrote a letter in Persian verse to the emperor Aurangzeb, a letter Sikhs call the Zafarnama. It names wrongs done to the Guru and his Sikhs, and it speaks of God and of broken promises.
Someone had to carry it across a great distance, toward the emperor in the south. Tradition says that was Bhai Daya Singh. Set the two moments side by side.

The first time, he rose from a crowd to face a sword. The second time, he rode toward an emperor's court with a letter that accused that court of breaking its word. Both times, someone had to go first, and it was him.
Bhai is a title of respect, brother. He's remembered as the brother who stood up before anyone else did.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh as the first of the Panj Pyare in the Vaisakhi story, and the Zafarnama is read and discussed in Sikh gatherings and schools.

o: the last of the five, who joined after the others
the scribe who wrote out the Guru's Persian letter
the first of the five to rise when the Guru asked for a head

games.q: the one who stood first — tap the pairs.
p: the Guru's letter in Persian verse

s: Daya Ram knew what was waiting in the tent
he rose without knowing; no one had gone before him.
tradition says he carried the Zafarnama to the emperor
the Guru's letter to Aurangzeb, carried toward the emperor's camp.

games.q: you're in the crowd at Anandpur. the Guru, sword drawn, asks for someone ready to give his head. nobody moves. what do you do?
o: wait to see if anyone else goes.
games.why: Daya Ram stood first, and four more followed. all five walked out of the tent as the Panj Pyare.

practice: Bring to mind one place where something needs doing and everyone is waiting for someone else: a mess in a shared kitchen, a neighbor who needs a hand, a family conversation nobody wants to start.
Picture yourself being the first to move, not dramatically, just standing up, and notice what makes you hesitate. Let the breath carry you through it.

wordCard.voice: Daya Singh. The first of the Panj Pyare to rise when the Guru asked for a head, and, tradition says, the one who carried the Zafarnama to the emperor. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bhai Daya Singh; bhai, brother, is a Sikh title of respect.

carryVoice: Your line: first to rise. Four more followed him out of that crowd. See you tomorrow.
